summary:
Mexico City recorded 17 homicides of LGBT+ people in 2024, 11 of them trans women, the highest raw state count in the country that year and the first time the city has led the count, according to annual monitoring published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective. These are raw counts. The sources supply no per-capita denominator and no general homicide rate for the city, so the figure cannot be presented as a rate or as a measure of risk relative to other jurisdictions.

The city's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct offence in the local penal code in July 2024, reported as 18 July and 19 July in different sources. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016, and made Mexico City the second state to create the offence. Article 148-Ter, added to the code on 23 August 2024, defines transfeminicidio as the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression.

In December 2024 the city created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit. Its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people.

The prosecution-service agreement FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide cases alongside feminicide investigations.

On 25 August 2025 the mayor launched a Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the city. The sources do not state whether its remit covers trans women.
tangentialFactors:
The state-count comparison is by raw count only. Mexico City's 17 homicides and Nuevo León's five are not adjusted for population, and no per-capita figures appear in the inventory; a populous jurisdiction accumulates more incidents than a small one for that reason alone, and the ranking cannot establish that any one state is more dangerous per resident.

The two principal figures come from different instruments. The annual count is civil-society monitoring of LGBT+ homicides, while article 148-Ter is a prosecutorial category in the local penal code; the inventory contains no figure tying the monitoring count to charges brought under the offence.
localsOnly: In July 2007 the Mexico City prison system began allowing conjugal visits between partners of the same sex, under a 2003 local law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The visiting partner was not required to be married to the inmate, and the change applied to all Mexico City prisons. The source attributes the change to the efforts of the human rights commission it identifies as the CDHDF.
outOfScopeNotes:
The prison source gives no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in Mexico City, on placement by birth sex versus identity, or on special units and segregation practice; it also does not say how the prison system classifies a trans partner for conjugal-visit purposes.

Unresolved: no figure in the inventory records how many transfeminicide cases have been charged or convicted under article 148-Ter, nor how the Gender Police has handled complaints involving trans women.
